claims.text: The initial eutectic high-entropy alloy has dual-phase lamellar colonies.
A heterogeneous grain structure can be introduced into the eutectic high-entropy alloy.
Introducing a heterogeneous grain structure will improve the alloy's strength relative to the unmodified lamellar-colony baseline.
Introducing a heterogeneous grain structure will improve room-temperature tensile ductility relative to the unmodified lamellar-colony baseline.
A heterogeneous grain structure induces load partitioning.
A heterogeneous grain structure induces strain-gradient hardening.
The heterogeneous grain structure causes dislocation pile-ups at grain boundaries.
The heterogeneous grain structure generates geometrically necessary dislocations.
Dislocation pile-ups and geometrically necessary dislocations create large, long-range internal back stresses.
Long-range internal back stresses sustain strain hardening.
Electromagnetic levitation melting, homogenization, hot forging, cold rolling, and partial-recrystallization annealing can produce a heterogeneous grain structure.
The target heterogeneous structure must be achieved through a specific processing route.
The optimal processing parameters and grain-structure characteristics for the target alloy are unknown.
The hypothesis can be tested by comparing specimens with and without the heterogeneous grain structure under otherwise identical tensile-test conditions.
Failure to improve both strength and ductility would falsify the stated joint-improvement hypothesis.
